title: Regina Caeli
hookLine: in Eastertide it replaces the Angelus: rejoice, he is risen

cards: Noon, and somewhere a church bell rings. For much of the year, the prayer that goes with that bell is the Angelus, which you met on day one hundred three: an angel, a young woman, a yes, and the Word made flesh.
But from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who keep the noon bell set the Angelus aside and pray something else. The story has jumped to its ending, and the prayer jumps with it.
It's short, and every line ends in the same word, like a door that keeps swinging open: alleluia. Today's word is the Easter prayer to Mary, Regina Caeli.

teach.h: THE FIRST WORD TO HER: REJOICE.
teach.b: In plain English: queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For he whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia, has risen, as he said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia.

Start with the first command: rejoice, in Latin laetare. Think back this week to the woman who stood at the cross, whose soul Simeon said a sword would pierce. In the Easter prayer, the first thing said to her is be glad.
The one who knew the worst of Friday is told about Sunday.

Then the two Latin words in the middle that carry the weight: sicut dixit, as he said. They echo the angel at the empty tomb in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said."
The prayer doesn't only announce that he rose. It says he kept his word. A promise made before the cross turns out true on the other side of it.
Then the alleluias. Through Lent, the Latin Church sets the word alleluia aside; it isn't sung at Mass.
At Easter it comes back, and this little prayer can't stop saying it.
Last, it still asks: pray for us to God.

teach.h: HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN, AS HE SAID.
teach.b: Even at the height of joy, it turns to Mary for help, the way this whole week has. So in Easter the noon bell rings for a mother told to rejoice because her son kept his promise.

how: In the Easter season, from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who pray the Angelus at morning, noon and evening say the Regina Caeli in its place, and it also closes Night Prayer through that season.

games.q: you're one of the women at the empty tomb on Sunday morning. an angel speaks. what does he say?
o: he is not here, for he is risen, as he said.
wait here, and he will come back.
games.why: Matthew 28:6. the Regina Caeli borrows its last words, sicut dixit, as he said: a promise kept.

practice: Bring to mind one promise someone made to you and kept, a friend who showed up, a call returned, and remember the moment you knew they'd kept it; then let it widen: as he said.
If you pray, say the Regina Caeli slowly now, with an alleluia at the end of each line. If you don't, hold that kept promise in mind and let it be good news.

wordCard.voice: Regina Caeli. Queen of heaven: the Easter prayer, rejoice, he is risen. This week's road: many names, poetry for a mother, comfort of the afflicted, mother of the church, star of the sea, hail, queen of heaven, and now rejoice.

orig.note: Latin: queen of heaven, rejoice, the prayer's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: queen of heaven, rejoice. He kept his word. Alleluia, and see you tomorrow.
